### II.4 BRD4 multivalency sharpens acetylation dependence of co-condensation

We now examine how BRD4 multivalency influences the sensitivity of co-condensation to acetylation density. Throughout this analysis, chromatin tension is held fixed below the critical value at $F\approx$1.26\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{N}$$ so that assembly can proceed via co-condensation. We then vary the acetylation probability $p_{\text{Ac}}$ along a segment of $N_{\text{Ac}}=20$ nucleosomes.

At this low tension, stable assemblies form only above a threshold acetylation probability $p_{\text{thr}}$ , with co-condensation occurring well below bulk coexistence when $p_{\text{Ac}}>p_{\text{thr}}$ . This sharp dependence of co-condensation on $p_{\text{Ac}}$ enables strong discrimination between highly acetylated regions ( $p_{\text{Ac}}\sim 0.7$ – $0.8$ ) and chromatin with modest background acetylation levels ( $p_{\text{Ac}}\sim 0.1$ – $0.15$ ) [32]. Importantly, for wild-type (WT) BRD4, $p_{\text{thr}}$ lies between $p_{\text{Ac}}\approx 0.4$ and $0.6$ over approximately an order of magnitude variation in the far-field BRD4 concentration below coexistence (Fig. 4a). The weak dependence of $p_{\text{thr}}$ on $S$ indicates that this discrimination remains robust to variations in BRD4 concentration when $S\gtrsim 0.1$ .

To isolate the role of multivalency in co-condensation, we compare WT BRD4, which has two active Ac-binding BDs, with a single-active-domain variant (mBD2). In the mBD2 model, both BD beads are retained sterically, but BD2--Ac binding is disabled and the BD1--Ac interaction strength is modestly adjusted to approximately match the effective BRD4--histone binding affinity of WT at intermediate acetylation ( $p_{\text{Ac}}\approx 0.5$ ; see Fig. S9). Although both models can co-condense with acetylated chromatin at sufficiently high $p_{\text{Ac}}$ and $S$ , their acetylation dependence differs in how the threshold behavior varies with saturation (Fig. 4a). In particular, mBD2 fails to form stable assemblies at any acetylation level when $S\lesssim 0.1$ , and its threshold acetylation probability $p_{\text{thr}}$ varies more strongly with $S$ at higher saturations where co-condensation can occur. Thus, multivalency does not simply shift the threshold for co-condensation but instead sharpens its dependence on acetylation density.

These differences in thresholding behavior arise from combinatorial binding effects [33, 34, 35]. Because each nucleosome contains multiple acetylatable histone tails, the typical number of distinct configurations in which a BRD4 molecule can bind a nucleosome increases with acetylation density. The number of binding configurations grows more rapidly for multivalent BRD4 than for the single-active-domain mBD2 variant, so that the favorable free-energy change due to binding varies more steeply with $p_{\text{Ac}}$ for WT BRD4 and reduces the sensitivity of the onset of co-condensation to BRD4 saturation. This mechanism is supported by a combinatorial binding model and by simulations at high chromatin tension that isolate BRD4–histone interactions from co-condensation (see SI Section S3 and Fig. S10).

Consistent with this mechanism, increasing the number of active BDs from one to two roughly doubles the slope of the co-condensation boundary when plotted as $\ln S$ versus acetylation probability for $S\gtrsim 0.1$ (Fig. 4a and Fig. S11). Multivalency therefore sharpens the boundary between co-condensed and non-assembling regimes and expands the range of subsaturated BRD4 concentrations over which co-condensation occurs. These effects enhance contrast between highly acetylated and weakly acetylated regions while increasing robustness to variations in BRD4 concentration.

### II.5 Co-condensation enables rapid assembly over a wide range of BRD4 concentrations

To understand how co-condensation modifies the kinetics of BRD4 assembly, we compare assembly formation rates above and below coexistence to the predictions of classical nucleation theory (CNT). We measure the rate density $j$ for finite assembly formation ( $S<1$ ) or condensed-phase nucleation ( $S>1$ ) as a function of $S$ and $p_{\text{Ac}}$ . We then define the dimensionless diffusion-normalized rate density $\tilde{j}=j\,t_{\rm Diff}(S)/(c_{\mathrm{coex}}S^{2/3})$ to compare rates across conditions, where $t_{\rm Diff}(S)=(2R_{\rm g})^{2}/[6D(S)]$ is the characteristic time for a BRD4 molecule to traverse its gyration diameter (Fig. S12). This normalization accounts for both the saturation dependence of molecular diffusion and the expected concentration dependence associated with diffusion over the mean intermolecular spacing. With this normalization, CNT predicts a strongly saturation-dependent nucleation barrier near coexistence, such that the diffusion-normalized rate obeys $\ln\tilde{j}=A-B/(\ln S)^{2}$ , with $S>1$ and $B>0$ [24].

We perform all kinetic simulations in the $NP_{x}P_{y}L_{z}T$ ensemble so that depletion of the far-field BRD4 reservoir does not appreciably influence the measured formation rates. For nucleation calculations at $S>1$ , $S$ denotes the supersaturation of the initially homogeneous BRD4 phase in which $c_{\rm far}=c=Sc_{\mathrm{coex}}$ prior to nucleation; following nucleation, growth of a post-critical cluster would ultimately lead to macroscopic phase separation. By contrast, under subsaturated conditions, $S$ describes both the initial and equilibrium far-field concentration since co-condensation leads to a finite BRD4 assembly.

Classical nucleation behavior is observed for homogeneous BRD4 phase separation in the absence of chromatin and for heterogeneous nucleation in the presence of high-tension chromatin, where co-condensation is suppressed (Fig. 5a). With $S>1$ , we extract the rate from the mean first-passage time to exceed a cluster size corresponding to post-critical growth. We then compute the rate density $j$ using the appropriate normalization volume for the process being measured; for chromatin-containing simulations, the reported excess chromatin-associated rate density is obtained after accounting for the expected homogeneous contribution in the accessible volume (see SI Section S4). In this high-tension regime, chromatin acts as a rigid substrate that lowers the heterogeneous nucleation barrier but does not alter the underlying CNT mechanism. Accordingly, the heterogeneous nucleation rate increases strongly with saturation and acetylation density, and its dependence on $S$ follows the CNT scaling expected for barrier-limited nucleation. Thus, high-tension chromatin can enhance nucleation locally, but the assembly kinetics exhibit extreme sensitivity to the bulk BRD4 concentration.

At low chromatin tension, where co-condensation is permitted, assembly proceeds via a qualitatively different mechanism (Fig. 5b). We define the total assembly formation rate as $J=1/\langle t_{\text{1st-passage}}\rangle$ , where $t_{\text{1st-passage}}$ is the earliest time at which the assembly size exceeds the threshold used to identify the formation of a stable assembly; $J$ is then converted to a rate density $j$ for a target region containing 20 acetylated nucleosomes (see SI Section S4). Stable assemblies form over a broad range of subsaturations, and formation rates vary only weakly with $S$ once acetylation exceeds the threshold required for stability. In contrast to nucleation-limited dynamics, assembly does not require the formation of a large critical assembly whose size depends strongly on concentration. Instead, BRD4 molecules adsorb onto chromatin and reorganize together with the polymer into a stable assembly, with the rate primarily limited by the diffusion of dilute BRD4 to the acetylated region over a broad range of subsaturations. Consistent with this picture, the diffusion-normalized rate densities $\tilde{j}$ are nearly constant across saturation conditions in this regime, indicating that assembly kinetics are set primarily by transport rather than by a large nucleation barrier. Co-condensation therefore tends to decouple rapid assembly formation rates from BRD4 saturation.

The influence of multivalency on kinetics parallels its effect on the equilibrium stability of BRD4 assemblies. Comparison with the single-active-domain mBD2 variant (Fig. 5c) shows that multivalency extends the regime of rapid assembly to lower saturation and reduces the residual dependence of assembly formation rates on saturation above $p_{\text{thr}}$ . While both models exhibit accelerated assembly at high $p_{\text{Ac}}$ , mBD2 assembles over a narrower subsaturated regime and exhibits slower assembly at lower $S$ , consistent with the reduced stability of co-condensation at low $S$ in the equilibrium analysis. Thus, multivalent binding enhances not only the thermodynamic robustness of co-condensation but also its kinetic accessibility.

The dependence of assembly rates on acetylation density further reinforces this connection between the kinetics and stability of co-condensation (Fig. 6). At high chromatin tension (Fig. 6a), rates increase steadily with $p_{\text{Ac}}$ when $S>1$ , reflecting progressive lowering of the heterogeneous nucleation barrier. By contrast, at low tension (Fig. 6b), rates increase sharply once $p_{\text{Ac}}$ exceeds the threshold for stable co-condensation and then plateau across a wide range of saturations, including deeply subsaturated conditions. This plateau reflects approximately diffusion-limited assembly and mirrors the thresholding behavior observed in equilibrium. For the single-active-domain mBD2 model (Fig. 6c), the plateau is weaker and assembly rates are more strongly suppressed at low $S$ , again consistent with mBD2’s co-condensation behavior in equilibrium.

To estimate absolute assembly times, we calibrate the simulation dynamics using the experimentally measured intranuclear diffusion coefficient of freely diffusing BRD4 (see SI Section S2.1 and Section S4.4). This mapping gives a characteristic BRD4 diffusion time of approximately $4.4\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{s}$ over one molecular diameter. The plateau co-condensation rates in Figs. 5 and 6 then correspond to a mean assembly-formation time of approximately $$20\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$\times S^{-2/3}$ for a target region containing 20 acetylated nucleosomes. At $S=0.1$ , this yields a mean assembly-formation time of approximately $90\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$ . Thus, stable BRD4 assemblies are predicted to form on subsecond timescales even under strongly subsaturated conditions. Although a direct quantitative comparison is complicated by differences in the number of available target sites and experimental detection thresholds, this predicted timescale is compatible with the rapid, seconds-scale formation of BRD4 condensates observed in U2OS cells [16].

Taken together, these results connect the kinetics of co-condensation to the same physical ingredients that determine its equilibrium behavior. Multivalency sharpens acetylation-dependent thresholds and expands the range of conditions under which co-condensation can occur, resulting in approximately diffusion-limited assembly that is not controlled by a large nucleation barrier. Consequently, co-condensation supports rapid assembly in the same parameter regime that enables strong discrimination between target and background chromatin while remaining robust to variations in BRD4 concentration.

We finally combine these equilibrium and kinetic analyses to identify the parameter regimes in which BRD4 can strongly discriminate between highly acetylated target regions and background chromatin while remaining robust to variations in BRD4 concentration and assembling on biologically relevant timescales. For a single acetylated chromatin region embedded in a nucleus of accessible volume $V_{\text{nucleus}}$ , preferential targeting requires that the total target-associated formation rate exceed the total off-target rate. Using $j_{\text{on}}$ to denote the excess chromatin-associated rate density above the homogeneous background rate density $j_{\text{off}}$ , the target-associated rate is $(j_{\text{on}}+j_{\text{off}})v$ , where $v$ is the effective target volume. Thus, preferential targeting requires

$$ (j_{\text{on}}+j_{\text{off}})v\gg j_{\text{off}}(V_{\text{nucleus}}-v). $$

For $V_{\text{nucleus}}/v\gg 1$ , this condition reduces to

$$ j_{\text{on}}v\gg j_{\text{off}}V_{\text{nucleus}}, $$

which is the targeting criterion used below. For a nucleus of radius $\sim$6\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{m}$$ and a single submicron-scale acetylated region, the ratio $V_{\text{nucleus}}/v$ can approach $10^{6}$ . Thus, in a supersaturated system, heterogeneous nucleation would require orders-of-magnitude enhancement of the local rate to overcome the larger off-target volume. At the same time, $j_{\text{on}}v$ must be sufficiently large in absolute terms to ensure rapid assembly following changes in acetylation.

These requirements are difficult to satisfy under high chromatin tension, where co-condensation is suppressed and assembly proceeds via classical heterogeneous nucleation (Fig. 7a). Because nucleation rates depend steeply on supersaturation, selective targeting occurs only in a small interval slightly above $S=1$ . Near-coexistence nucleation is slow everywhere, whereas at larger $S$ off-target nucleation becomes competitive. Moreover, the dependence of assembly on acetylation density in this regime is continuous rather than threshold-like, so modest background acetylation can promote nucleation at sufficiently high saturation. This narrow regime of sensitivity implies that targeting is not robust to fluctuations in BRD4 concentration, which are inevitable because growth toward macroscopic phase separation locally depletes dilute BRD4 and generates concentration gradients that couple distinct nucleation sites [36].

By contrast, when chromatin tension is sufficiently low to permit co-condensation, this mechanism instead defines a qualitatively different regime for spatiotemporal targeting (Fig. 7b). In subsaturated conditions ( $S<1$ ), off-chromatin nucleation of the bulk condensed phase is thermodynamically forbidden within this model, so $j_{\text{off}}=0$ for the bulk-nucleation process considered here. Stable assembly then requires exceeding a threshold acetylation density $p_{\text{thr}}\approx 0.5$ , which persists for WT BRD4 over approximately an order of magnitude variation in subsaturated concentration. This produces strong discrimination between highly acetylated regions and background chromatin with lower but nonzero acetylation. Because co-condensation in this regime is both thermodynamically stable and kinetically rapid—with a predicted mean assembly time of approximately $90\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$ at $S=0.1$ for a target region containing 20 acetylated nucleosomes—assemblies can form efficiently in response to changes in acetylation while maintaining strong target–background discrimination over variations in the far-field BRD4 concentration.

Comparison with the single-active-domain mBD2 model (Fig. 7c) highlights the role of multivalency in achieving sensitivity to acetylation density. Although mBD2 also supports co-condensation at low tension, the range of subsaturated conditions that lead to stable and rapid assembly is reduced relative to WT BRD4. Moreover, the threshold acetylation density varies more strongly with saturation than for WT BRD4, reducing the robustness of discrimination between highly acetylated regions and background chromatin. Thus, multivalency enhances the ability of co-condensation to distinguish between highly acetylated regions and background chromatin while preserving robustness to variations in BRD4 concentration.

## III Conclusions

We have identified a physical regime in which BRD4 assemblies strongly discriminate highly acetylated chromatin from chromatin with lower background acetylation. Building on prior theoretical studies of co-condensation [25, 28, 27, 26, 22, 23], we address the question of whether this mechanism can provide the degree of spatial selectivity required for chromatin targeting without requiring fine-tuned protein concentrations. Our ultra-coarse-grained molecular-dynamics model demonstrates that the interplay of subsaturation, chromatin mechanics, and multivalent binding defines a parameter regime in which finite BRD4 assemblies form rapidly at highly acetylated regions while suppressing off-target aggregation. In this regime, strong discrimination between target and background chromatin and robustness to concentration fluctuations emerge simultaneously rather than being in competition.

Our results also help clarify the physical description of chromatin-associated condensates. The targeting regime characterized here differs from polymer bridging [37] or collapse driven solely by 1:1 binding interactions [38, 39], as it requires that BRD4 possess the intrinsic capacity to phase separate at sufficiently high concentrations through IDR-mediated self-attraction, which is strongest in the C-terminal region. Nonetheless, this mechanism does not entail bulk phase separation; rather, it defines a regime in which BRD4 assemblies exist as finite, chromatin-associated structures that are stabilized by the combined effects of binding and self-attraction. This regime enables selective and rapid targeting because assembly occurs under subsaturated conditions with approximately diffusion-limited kinetics rather than being controlled by a large nucleation barrier, while multivalent binding maintains strong discrimination between acetylation levels over a broad range of BRD4 concentrations.

These findings underscore the nuance required when interpreting signatures of phase separation in the context of chromatin [8, 40, 41, 42, 43, 11, 44, 45, 46]. Features often associated with phase separation—such as thresholded assembly or droplet-like morphology—do not necessarily imply classical nucleation mechanisms or macroscopic demixing. Conversely, the absence of coarsening or large-scale phase separation does not preclude a thermodynamic origin rooted in intermolecular attractions that drive phase separation at higher concentrations. Our work further highlights qualitative differences between the formation kinetics of finite chromatin-associated assemblies and the classical nucleation kinetics of phase-separated droplets.

These predicted requirements for selective and concentration-robust targeting can be tested experimentally by varying chromatin acetylation density and global BRD4 concentration while monitoring assembly at defined chromatin regions. Our simulation results can also be validated by perturbing BRD4 valency to test its predicted role in maintaining discrimination across concentrations. Although the present model omits additional nuclear components and crowding effects, the core mechanism is not expected to depend qualitatively on these details. Incorporating such factors will be important for understanding how chromatin-associated BRD4 assemblies recruit downstream transcriptional machinery and operate within the broader nuclear environment.

## S1 Ultra-coarse-grained (UCG) model of BRD4 and chromatin

Energies are expressed in units of the thermal energy $k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ , so that $k_{\mathrm{B}}T=1$ in reduced simulation units. The background solvent is represented implicitly; energies in the UCG model therefore represent potentials of mean force. Masses are normalized such that the total mass of a BRD4 molecule is $m_{\text{BRD4,WT}}=1$ .

### S1.1 Chromatin model and bonding interactions

Chromatin is modeled as a semiflexible polymer of nucleosomes connected by linker DNA. Each nucleosome is represented as a bead with fixed geometry, and neighboring nucleosomes are connected by modified FENE (finite extensible nonlinear elastic)-like bonds that enforce connectivity while allowing finite extensibility [47].

#### Bending potential.

A bending potential is applied to successive bonds between nucleosomes, indexed by $i$ ,

$$ \frac{U}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}=-B\sum_{i}\cos(\theta_{i+1}-\theta_{i}), $$

where $\theta_{i}$ is the orientation angle of bond $i$ and $B$ is the dimensionless bending stiffness. Matching to the continuum worm-like-chain model gives

$$ B=\frac{l_{\text{p}}^{\rm chromatin}}{\delta l}. $$

Using $l_{\text{p}}^{\rm chromatin}\approx$16.5\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ and $\delta l\approx$17.8\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ [48, 49], we obtain $B\approx 0.93$ , corresponding to a bending stiffness of approximately $0.93\,k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ .

We note that chromatin rigidity can, in principle, oppose collapse during co-condensation by introducing a mechanical barrier to bending. However, sensitivity tests show that this effect is negligible for biologically relevant parameters: only for $l_{\text{p}}^{\rm chromatin}/\delta l\gtrsim 20$ does bending rigidity significantly stabilize extended configurations and impede collapse. In the parameter regime considered here, chromatin mechanics are therefore well captured by the baseline choice $B\approx 0.93$ .

#### Bonding potential.

The bonding potential is

$$ \frac{U_{\text{bond}}(r)}{k_{\text{B}}T}=-\frac{KR_{0}^{2}}{2}\ln\left[1-\left(\frac{r-\Delta_{ij}}{R_{0}}\right)^{2}\right]+4\varepsilon\left[\left(\frac{\sigma_{ij}^{*}}{r}\right)^{12}-\left(\frac{\sigma_{ij}^{*}}{r}\right)^{6}\right], $$

where $\Delta_{ij}=\sigma_{ij}^{*}=(\sigma_{i}^{*}+\sigma_{j}^{*})/2$ offsets the effective attachment points between beads $i$ and $j$ to account for finite bead size, $\sigma_{i}^{*}$ denotes the hard-core diameter of bead $i$ , and $\varepsilon=1$ sets the repulsive energy scale. This form is a modified FENE bond. Whereas the standard FENE potential [47] assumes that bonds connect particle centers, bead diameters are comparable to bond lengths in the present model, so that a center-to-center connection would lead to unphysical overlap and incorrect geometry. To account for the bead size, the effective attachment points of the bond are shifted by $\Delta_{ij}$ , which can be interpreted as moving the endpoints of the spring from bead centers toward their surfaces. With this modification, the maximal bond extension becomes $R_{0}+\Delta_{ij}$ , ensuring physically meaningful separation between bonded beads. The same bonding potential is used consistently for both chromatin linkers and protein domains connected by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), providing a unified treatment of connectivity across the model.

Chromatin linker lengths are set by the number of DNA base pairs in the linker, $R_{0}=L_{\mathrm{linker}}=N_{\mathrm{bp}}l_{\mathrm{bp}}$ , where $l_{\mathrm{bp}}=$0.34\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ [50]. For U2OS cells, which we take as a representative system, we use $N_{\mathrm{bp}}\sim 40$ , giving $R_{0}\approx$14\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ . Chromatin stiffness is parameterized using a persistence length $l_{\text{p}}^{\rm chromatin}=$16.5\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ [48]. We estimate the chromatin rigidity parameter $K$ from the persistence length using $K=3/(2l_{\text{p}}^{\rm chromatin}L_{\mathrm{linker}})$ , which relates the spring constant for small end-to-end distance fluctuations to the worm-like-chain variance in the short-linker limit. The chromatin rigidity parameter $K$ , initially estimated as $6.4\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-2}$ , is scaled down by a factor of approximately $0.7$ to better match the experimental nucleosome–nucleosome distance distribution (Fig. S2). To conserve the steric volume of a nucleosome disk of thickness $6.5\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ and diameter $11\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ [29], we use an effective nucleosome diameter $\sigma^{*}=$10.6\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ .

#### Nucleosome geometry and acetylation.

Each nucleosome contains eight histone tails in total, of which two H3 and two H4 tails are acetylatable. To represent their spatial organization, we place tail attachment points approximately at the vertices of a cube surrounding the nucleosome core [29]. This geometry captures the roughly isotropic distribution of tails while preventing artificial clustering. To maintain this arrangement, we introduce 12 weak angular constraints between tail–nucleosome–tail triplets corresponding to the edges of the cube. These constraints are chosen to be minimal, serving only to prevent collapse of tails toward a single side of the nucleosome (e.g., toward a nearby BRD4-rich region) while preserving sufficient flexibility for realistic binding configurations.

Acetylation (Ac) is introduced on a segment of $N_{\text{Ac}}$ consecutive nucleosomes. Each H3 and H4 tail is acetylated independently with probability $p_{\text{Ac}}$ unless otherwise specified. To connect $N_{\text{Ac}}$ to experimentally observed chromatin organization, we estimate the typical number of consecutively acetylated nucleosomes from genomic data. Acetylated regions in human cells span a wide range of lengths, from $\sim$100\text{\,}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{p}$$ in small enhancers to $>$50\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{p}$$ in super-enhancers [30, 31], with a substantial fraction of peaks in the range $\sim 1$ – $6\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{p}$ [31]. A nucleosome wraps $\sim$150\text{\,}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{p}$$ of DNA, and linker DNA typically contributes an additional $\sim 10$ – $80\text{\,}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{p}$ [31]. For U2OS cells, the linker length of $\sim$40\text{\,}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{p}$$ gives $\sim$190\text{\,}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{p}$$ per nucleosome. This correspondence implies that acetylated regions of $\sim 1$ – $6\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{p}$ span approximately $5$ – $30$ consecutive nucleosomes. Guided by this estimate, we use $N_{\text{Ac}}=20$ in the main text and also consider $N_{\text{Ac}}=30$ in the supplementary figures.

To limit Ac density fluctuations, we use a “shuffle” acetylation scheme, in which a fixed number $4p_{\text{Ac}}N_{\text{Ac}}$ of acetylated tails are randomly distributed among the $4N_{\text{Ac}}$ sites. This removes fluctuations in the overall acetylation density while preserving local randomness. This scheme is motivated by the strong sensitivity of observables near the acetylation threshold for co-condensation $p_{\text{Ac}}\approx p_{\text{thr}}$ , where fluctuations in the total number of acetylated tails significantly affect quantities such as the average assembly size.

### S1.2 BRD4 model and IDR-mediated interactions

#### Molecular geometry and excluded volume.

Each BRD4 molecule is represented by three beads corresponding to BD1, BD2, and the C-terminal domain. This representation is motivated by the domain architecture of BRD4, which contains two bromodomains (BD1 and BD2) responsible for binding acetylated histone tails, and a C-terminal structured domain embedded within extended IDRs [16]. Domain boundaries and structured regions are identified from AlphaFold2 structural predictions [51], using high-confidence segments to define globular domains and assigning intervening regions to IDRs. Effective sizes $\sigma_{i}^{*}$ of globular domains are determined from these structural models by matching their volumes. For each domain, atoms corresponding to the selected amino-acid range are used to construct an inertia tensor, which is then mapped to an equivalent uniform ellipsoid. The resulting effective diameter $\sigma_{i}^{*}$ is defined such that the ellipsoid volume is preserved, providing a consistent measure of steric size across domains. Steric parameters are chosen not only to prevent overlap but also to reproduce physically reasonable condensed-phase densities. Accordingly, effective bead sizes incorporate both globular domain volume and associated IDR volume, ensuring that excluded-volume interactions yield realistic packing in the dense phase.

To assign IDR segments to individual coarse-grained beads, we partition the full BRD4 amino-acid sequence based on the locations of structured domains. IDR regions are defined as the sequence segments between adjacent structured domains, with boundaries assigned at the midpoints between neighboring domain endpoints. Concretely, if structured domains have index ranges $[i^{*}_{\mathrm{beg}},i^{*}_{\mathrm{end}})$ , then the IDR associated with a given domain consists of all amino acids between the midpoint to the preceding domain and the midpoint to the following domain, excluding residues belonging to structured regions. This ensures that each amino acid in the sequence is uniquely assigned either to a globular domain or to a single IDR segment. This construction provides an unambiguous and systematic partitioning of the sequence, allowing the IDR length $N_{\text{IDR}}$ associated with each coarse-grained bead to be defined consistently from the underlying protein sequence.

To account for the contribution of IDRs, we construct their effective volume from amino-acid volumes,

$$ V_{\mathrm{IDR},i}=\frac{1}{0.7}\sum_{k\in\mathrm{IDR}_{i}}v_{\mathrm{AA},k}, $$

where $v_{\mathrm{AA},k}$ are residue-specific volumes [52] in solution. The prefactor $1/0.7$ accounts for hydration and imperfect packing, reflecting that IDRs in solution do not fill space at unit density but instead occupy an expanded, solvent-accessible volume. This construction corresponds to an approximate picture in which IDR segments compactify around structured domains in the dense phase while retaining a finite excluded volume set by their sequence composition.

Excluded-volume interactions are modeled using a Weeks–Chandler–Andersen (WCA) potential,

$$ \frac{U_{\text{WCA}}}{k_{\text{B}}T}=4\varepsilon\left[\left(\frac{\sigma_{ij}}{r}\right)^{12}-\left(\frac{\sigma_{ij}}{r}\right)^{6}\right]+U_{0},\quad r\leq R_{\text{cut}}, $$

with $\sigma_{ij}=(\sigma_{i}+\sigma_{j})/2$ and $\varepsilon=1$ . The offset $U_{0}$ is chosen to make $U_{\text{WCA}}(R_{\text{cut}}=2^{1/6}\sigma_{ij})=0$ . Effective bead sizes $\sigma_{i}$ are determined from their globular domain size $\sigma_{i}^{*}$ and IDR volume,

$$ \sigma_{i}=\left((\sigma_{i}^{*})^{3}+\frac{6V_{\mathrm{IDR},i}}{\pi}\right)^{1/3}. $$

#### Bonding potential.

Bonded interactions between the BRD4 beads follow Eq. (S3). For protein IDRs, the maximum extension is set by the contour length, $R_{0}=\ell_{\text{IDR}}=N_{\text{IDR}}l_{\text{AA}}$ , where $l_{\text{AA}}=$0.38\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ is the average spacing between amino acids [53, 54, 55]. The bond stiffness $K$ is chosen to reproduce small extension fluctuations of polymer segments. For IDR-mediated connections, this gives $K=3/(2l_{\text{p}}^{\rm IDR}\ell_{\text{IDR}})$ , where the IDR persistence length is $l_{\text{p}}^{\rm IDR}\approx$4\text{\,}\AA$$ .

#### IDR-mediated attractive interactions.

Non-specific attraction between IDR-containing beads is modeled using a Gaussian potential,

$$ \frac{U_{\text{gauss}}}{k_{\text{B}}T}=-Al_{\text{AA}}^{3}\frac{N_{\text{IDR}i}N_{\text{IDR}j}}{(R_{\text{g,i}}^{2}+R_{\text{g,j}}^{2})^{3/2}}\exp\left[-\frac{1.6r^{2}}{R_{\text{g,i}}^{2}+R_{\text{g,j}}^{2}}\right], $$

where $R_{\text{g,i}}^{2}=(\sigma_{i}^{*}/2)^{2}+l_{\text{p}}^{\rm IDR}l_{\text{AA}}N_{\text{IDR}i}/3$ . This interaction form is motivated by Flory-type polymer theory. The original derivation assumes that polymer chains adopt approximately Gaussian density profiles around their centers of mass [56], which leads to an effective interaction between chains proportional to the overlap of these densities. This framework was later generalized to interactions between heterogeneous chains of different sizes and compositions [57], yielding the form used here. The Gaussian factor therefore reflects the physical picture that IDRs behave as diffuse polymer blobs whose overlap generates an effective attraction. The numerical factor in the exponential, here taken as $1.6$ , arises from more detailed simulations of polymer chains beyond the idealized Gaussian model, which show that the effective interaction range is slightly shorter than predicted by the simplest theory [58].

The prefactor $A$ encodes the strength of the IDR-mediated interaction. This overall interaction strength is calibrated using corelet phase-separation experiments [59, 16]. Matching the observed critical valence of BRD4 corelets in those experiments yields $A\approx 0.105$ (Fig. S1).

### S1.3 BRD4–chromatin interactions

#### Binding strengths and dissociation constants.

Binding between BRD4 and chromatin is modeled as 1:1 interactions between bromodomains and acetylated histone tails. Binding strengths are derived from experimental dissociation constants [60] using

$$ \frac{U_{\text{bind}}}{k_{\text{B}}T}=-\ln\left(v_{0}K_{\text{d}}\right), $$

where $v_{0}$ is the interaction volume and $K_{\text{d}}$ is the dissociation constant. This expression can be understood from a balance between entropic and enthalpic contributions to binding. When a bromodomain binds an acetylated lysine, the molecule is effectively confined from a dilute volume $1/c$ to a binding volume $v_{0}$ , incurring an entropic penalty $\sim-\ln(cv_{0})$ . At equilibrium, this penalty is compensated by a free energy $U_{\text{bind}}$ , which by definition balances at $c=K_{\text{d}}$ , yielding $U_{\text{bind}}/k_{\text{B}}T=-\ln(v_{0}K_{\text{d}})$ . In applying this relation, we assume that bromodomains measured in isolation in titration experiments have approximately the same effective size and binding geometry as bromodomains within the full BRD4 molecule. We therefore estimate the interaction volume as $v_{0}\sim V_{\mathrm{BD}}=(\pi/6)(\sigma_{i}^{*})^{3}$ , corresponding to the volume of the coarse-grained globular domain.

Experimental measurements report four distinct dissociation constants for BD1/BD2 binding to H3/H4 tails [60]. These yield slightly different binding energies $U_{\text{BD1-H3}}:U_{\text{BD1-H4}}:U_{\text{BD2-H3}}:U_{\text{BD2-H4}}=6.57:5.56:5.55:6.58$ . Accounting for experimental uncertainty, we group them into two effective interaction strengths with the ratio $6.57:5.55$ corresponding to stronger and weaker binding pairs, preserving the overall scale while simplifying the model. Importantly, these values correspond to binding of a single acetylated lysine, whereas histone tails can contain multiple acetylation sites that contribute cooperatively to binding [61]. This motivates introducing an overall scaling factor to account for multivalent contributions along a single histone tail. We calibrate this factor by matching phase-separation behavior in corelet systems [16], choosing the minimal scaling that reliably produces phase separation at valence $v=2$ (Fig. S1). Calibration yields a multiplicative factor of $2.15$ ; this is consistent with the fact that the typical number of acetylations per histone tail is two, with some tails having more, yielding an expected enhancement in the effective binding strength by a factor slightly greater than two. This procedure ensures that relative binding affinities are preserved while the absolute scale is tuned to reproduce experimentally observed phase behavior.

#### Enforcement of 1:1 binding interactions.

To enforce strict 1:1 binding while maintaining numerical stability and minimal perturbation to the rest of the model, we implement the following modifications to the nonbonded interactions, Eq. (S5) and Eq. (S7), with explicit geometric and dynamical constraints:

- 1. Disable steric WCA repulsion between BD domains and acetylated tails, allowing an Ac tail to occupy the center of the binding pocket.

- 2. Introduce a Gaussian attraction with well depth $U_{\text{bind}}$ and a short interaction range. The range is chosen as $R_{\mathrm{bind}}\approx 0.34\sigma_{\mathrm{BDAc}}/2$ , where $\sigma_{\mathrm{BDAc}}=(\sigma_{\mathrm{BD}}+\sigma_{\mathrm{Ac}})/2$ , and $\sigma_{\mathrm{BD}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{Ac}}$ are the WCA diameters of a BD bead and an acetylated-tail bead, respectively. This choice ensures that the attraction is significantly shorter-ranged than the steric exclusion between BD domains. It therefore enforces geometric exclusivity: once an Ac tail binds and localizes near the center of a BD domain, other BD domains cannot approach closely enough to feel the binding potential. Steric repulsion limits the closest approach of two BD domains to $r\gtrsim\sigma_{\mathrm{BDBD}}$ , where $\sigma_{\mathrm{BDBD}}$ is the BD–BD WCA contact diameter; at this separation, $|U_{\text{bind}}(r)|\ll k_{\text{B}}T$ .

- 3. Introduce steric repulsion between acetylated tails with effective size $\sigma_{\mathrm{AcAc}}\approx 0.85\sigma_{\mathrm{BDBD}}$ . This prevents multiple Ac tails from simultaneously approaching a bound BD domain. The value is chosen as a compromise, as it is large enough to enforce single occupancy, but small enough to avoid artificially disrupting droplet structure or histone tail packing.

- 4. Extend the maximum bond length of histone tails from $\ell_{\text{IDR}}/2$ to $3\ell_{\text{IDR}}/4$ , where $\ell_{\text{IDR}}$ is the length of the IDR portion of the corresponding histone tail. Short linker lengths combined with nonlinear bond potentials would otherwise generate large forces over short distances, requiring prohibitively small integration timesteps. This extension reduces stiffness without altering the qualitative geometry of binding.

- 5. Increase the mass of acetylated tails to $m_{\mathrm{Ac}}\approx 0.6\,m_{\mathrm{BRD4}}$ . In the coarse-grained representation, tails would otherwise have very small mass, leading to large accelerations under strong, short-range binding forces. Increasing the mass stabilizes integration while primarily affecting dynamics rather than equilibrium properties, making it the least disruptive modification.

These combined modifications ensure strict 1:1 binding. Validation simulations comprising $\sim 1000$ BRD4 molecules and $\sim 800$ acetylated tails showed no violations of the 1:1 binding constraint.

Together, these elements define a minimal ultra-coarse-grained model capturing multivalent binding, self-attraction, and chromatin mechanics required for BRD4 assembly.

## S2 Simulation methods

All simulations are implemented in LAMMPS [62]. Different ensembles are utilized for distinct simulation purposes, as described below. In all simulations, we use a Langevin thermostat [63] with damping time constant $\tau_{\text{Langevin}}=10$ in reduced simulation units. This value is chosen as a compromise between maintaining sufficiently rapid diffusion for efficient sampling and limiting the concentration dependence of the BRD4 diffusion coefficient $D(S)$ arising from intermolecular collisions.

### S2.1 Calibration of dynamical timescales

To map the simulated dynamics to physical timescales, we use the experimentally measured intranuclear diffusion coefficient of freely diffusing BRD4, $D_{\rm exp}=$5.4(\pm 0.3)\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s}$$ [64]. As an independent order-of-magnitude consistency check, the measured intranuclear viscosity, $\eta\approx$4(\pm 1)\text{\,}\mathrm{c}\mathrm{P}$$ [65], together with the Stokes–Einstein relation [66, 67] and an effective hydrodynamic radius $R_{\rm h}\sim R_{\rm g}\approx$6\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ , gives $D\approx$9.3(\pm 2.4)\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s}$$ . Using the direct experimental measurement of $D_{\rm exp}$ for the quantitative calibration, we obtain a characteristic timescale for a BRD4 molecule to diffuse one molecular diameter,

$$ t_{\rm Diff}^{\rm exp}=\frac{(2R_{\rm g})^{2}}{6D_{\rm exp}}\approx$4.4(\pm 0.3)\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{s}$. $$

We use this calibration to convert the assembly timescales measured in simulations to physical units; given the experimental and modeling uncertainties, we consider these timescales to be order-of-magnitude estimates. This procedure avoids assigning physical significance to the bare molecular-dynamics time unit and instead calibrates the kinetic observables directly to the experimentally measured BRD4 mobility.

### S2.2 $NVT$ simulations of bulk coexistence

Bulk phase behavior is characterized using constant-volume ( $NVT$ ) simulations. Systems are initialized with uniform BRD4 concentration and evolved until phase separation occurs, yielding coexisting dilute and condensed phases. The dilute-phase concentration $c_{\mathrm{coex}}$ is determined from the equilibrium density of the dilute region in the absence of chromatin.

In simulations with chromatin, the chromatin fiber spans the simulation box under periodic boundary conditions along the $z$ direction, ensuring coexistence between phases in direct contact with the polymer. Concentration profiles are computed by averaging particle concentrations along the $z$ axis after equilibration.

### S2.3 Determination of the coexistence concentration $c_{\mathrm{coex}}$

The coexistence concentration $c_{\mathrm{coex}}$ is determined from $NVT$ simulations of BRD4 in the absence of chromatin. Systems are initialized at concentrations above coexistence and allowed to phase separate into coexisting dilute and condensed phases. The dilute-phase concentration is measured by averaging the BRD4 density in regions far from the condensed phase after equilibration. To reduce finite-size effects, measurements are performed over multiple independent simulations and averaged over time once equilibrium coexistence is established. The resulting value of $c_{\mathrm{coex}}$ is used to define the saturation ratio $S=c_{\rm far}/c_{\mathrm{coex}}$ throughout the main text.

### S2.4 $NP_{x}P_{y}L_{z}T$ ensemble and chromatin tension control

To control the far-field BRD4 concentration and chromatin mechanics independently, we perform simulations in an $NP_{x}P_{y}L_{z}T$ ensemble. We use this ensemble for both equilibrium simulations of chromatin-associated assemblies at subsaturated conditions ( $S<1$ ) and kinetic measurements of assembly formation and condensed-phase nucleation rates below ( $S<1$ ) and above ( $S>1$ ) coexistence, respectively. This simulation approach suppresses finite-simulation-volume artifacts due to BRD4 depletion while still producing continuous trajectories with Langevin dynamics, as described below.

In this ensemble, the number of particles $N$ , temperature $T$ , and box length $L_{z}$ are fixed, while the lateral box dimensions $L_{x}$ and $L_{y}$ fluctuate under control of the corresponding pressures $P_{x}$ and $P_{y}$ . Periodic boundary conditions are applied in all three directions. Because the chromatin fiber spans the simulation box along the $z$ direction, $L_{z}$ is excluded from the barostat so that the mechanical constraint imposed on the chromatin is not coupled directly to the pressure used to control the far-field BRD4 concentration.

In the simulation conditions considered in this work, both the far-field BRD4 concentration at subsaturated conditions ( $S<1$ ) and the initially homogeneous BRD4 concentration at supersaturated conditions prior to nucleation ( $S>1$ ) are well approximated by the ideal equation of state,

$$ P_{\rm gas}\simeq c_{\rm far}k_{\mathrm{B}}T. $$

We therefore impose the lateral pressures

$$ P_{x}=P_{y}=Sc_{\mathrm{coex}}k_{\mathrm{B}}T, $$

where $c_{\mathrm{coex}}$ is the dilute-phase BRD4 concentration at bulk coexistence obtained independently from $NVT$ direct-coexistence simulations. At subsaturated conditions ( $S<1$ ), the barostat enforces a far-field concentration

$$ c_{\rm far}\simeq Sc_{\mathrm{coex}} $$

throughout the simulation. For nucleation calculations at $S>1$ , the initially homogeneous system has $c=c_{\rm far}\simeq Sc_{\mathrm{coex}}$ prior to nucleation, while pressure control maintains the far-field concentration during the early stages of nucleation and post-critical growth; we terminate such simulations well before the condensed phase occupies the entire simulation volume.

Chromatin extension is controlled by the fixed box length $L_{z}$ . We define

$$ \lambda=\frac{N_{\text{H}}a_{\text{HH}}}{L_{z}}, $$

where $a_{\text{HH}}$ is the equilibrium spacing between neighboring nucleosomes. Large $\lambda$ corresponds to low initial chromatin tension and permits substantial local compaction, whereas $\lambda\approx 1$ corresponds to a nearly straight, high-tension fiber. The mapping between $\lambda$ and the resulting mechanical tension $F$ is obtained from independent simulations without BRD4 (Fig. S6). Although $P_{z}$ is not externally controlled, the far-field BRD4 gas equilibrates to an isotropic pressure tensor; however, because tension on the chromatin fiber also contributes to the $z$ component of the total stress tensor, the measured $P_{z}$ of the simulation box may not be exactly equal to $P_{x}$ and $P_{y}$ at equilibrium.

We directly validate the far-field concentration control in Fig. S5. For two representative values of $S<1$ , the BRD4 concentration measured sufficiently far from the chromatin and excluding the region surrounding the chromatin-associated assembly remains close to the target value $Sc_{\mathrm{coex}}$ both before and after assembly formation. This is accompanied by a decrease in the simulation-box volume of approximately $20\%$ at $S=0.3$ and $40\%$ at $S=0.9$ , as the lateral dimensions respond to sequestration of BRD4 into the finite assembly. The substantial volume response demonstrates that the constancy of $c_{\rm far}$ is maintained by the pressure-controlled ensemble rather than arising simply because assembly formation produces a negligible perturbation. As a further test, after the chromatin-associated assembly has equilibrated in the $NP_{x}P_{y}L_{z}T$ ensemble, we fix the simulation box at its equilibrated dimensions and continue the same configuration in the $NVT$ ensemble. The assembly and surrounding BRD4 gas show no appreciable change following this switch (Fig. S5), demonstrating that the equilibrated finite assembly is not stabilized artificially by continued pressure control.

### S2.5 Finite assembly stability and hysteresis

Assemblies are identified using a cluster-detection algorithm based on spatial proximity. Two BRD4 molecules are considered part of the same assembly if any pair of their constituent beads lies within a specified cutoff distance corresponding to the range of attractive interactions. The assembly size $N_{\text{cl}}$ is defined as the number of BRD4 molecules in the largest connected cluster. This definition is used consistently across equilibrium and kinetic analyses. Radial concentration profiles for finite assemblies are computed by averaging particle densities as a function of distance from the assembly center of mass. For bulk coexistence simulations, concentration profiles are computed along the $z$ direction. These measurements allow direct comparison between finite assemblies formed under subsaturated conditions and bulk condensed phases in direct-coexistence simulations.

The stability of finite BRD4 assemblies under subsaturated conditions is characterized by comparing simulations initialized with and without a pre-formed BRD4 cluster. In simulations initialized from a dispersed state, assembly formation is monitored to determine whether stable co-condensation occurs. In complementary simulations initialized with a pre-formed cluster, the persistence or dissolution of the assembly is used to determine the stability boundary. The separation between formation and dissolution conditions defines a hysteresis region associated with a finite free-energy barrier between the dispersed and assembled states.

### S2.6 Adaptive biasing force calculations of binding free-energy profiles

Adaptive biasing force (ABF) calculations are used to obtain BRD4–chromatin binding free-energy profiles under high-tension conditions, where chromatin deformation and co-condensation are suppressed. The specific ABF setup used to extract effective dissociation constants is described in Section S3. In these calculations, the collective variable is the center-of-mass distance between BRD4 bromodomains and acetylated tails, as defined in Eq. (S14).

## S3 Multivalency and combinatorial binding theory

### S3.1 Effective binding affinity and $K_{\text{d}}$ measurements

#### Inference via adsorption simulations.

To quantify BRD4–chromatin interactions in the coarse-grained model, we relate simulation binding parameters to experimentally measured dissociation constants $K_{\text{d}}$ [60]. To validate this mapping in the model, we perform simulations of BRD4 binding to chromatin under conditions where co-condensation is suppressed (high chromatin tension). Under these conditions, the measured occupancy of BRD4 on chromatin can be related directly to an effective $K_{\text{d}}$ . The effective dissociation constant is obtained by fitting the fraction of bound BRD4 molecules as a function of concentration to a standard adsorption isotherm. This procedure allows direct comparison between the wild-type (WT) BRD4 model and the single-active-domain mBD2 variant, ensuring that both models have approximately matched effective binding affinities at intermediate acetylation density ( $p_{\text{Ac}}\approx 0.5$ ), as described in the main text.

#### Direct calculation via ABF simulations.

To obtain $K_{\text{d}}$ directly from simulations, we perform explicit binding free-energy calculations using ABF simulations. The system consists of a single nucleosome at high tension ( $\lambda=1$ ) with controlled acetylation patterns and a single BRD4 molecule. Acetylation is assigned independently to H3 and H4 tails, allowing configurations corresponding to $p_{\text{Ac}}^{\mathrm{H3}},p_{\text{Ac}}^{\mathrm{H4}}\in\{0,0.5,1\}$ . This setup isolates BRD4–chromatin binding from co-condensation effects.

We define the ABF collective variable as the distance between the center of mass of the BRD4 bromodomains and the center of mass of the acetylated tails,

$$ r=\left|\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{CoM}}(\mathrm{BD1},\mathrm{BD2})-\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{CoM}}(\mathrm{Ac\ tails})\right|, $$

where $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{CoM}}(\mathrm{Ac\ tails})$ is computed over the acetylated H3 and H4 tails present in the simulation. We perform ABF sampling along this coordinate to obtain the free-energy profile $F(r)$ . A configuration is defined as bound if the minimum pairwise distance between any bromodomain and any acetylated tail satisfies

$$ r_{\text{min}}=\min_{i\in\mathrm{Ac},\,j\in\{\mathrm{BD1,BD2}\}}r_{ij}<R_{\text{top}}, $$

where $R_{\text{top}}$ is chosen to include the BD–Ac binding well while excluding configurations with more than one bromodomain participating in the interaction. The total binding probability in a system of finite size can be written as

$$ P_{\text{b}}=\int_{0}^{L}P(b\mid r)\,p(r)\,dr, $$

where $P(b\mid r)$ is the conditional probability of being bound at fixed $r$ and $p(r)$ is the equilibrium radial probability density. To properly normalize $p(r)$ , we define a modified free energy

$$ \tilde{F}^{3D}(r)=\frac{F(r)}{k_{\text{B}}T}+\ln\left[\left(\frac{r}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right], $$

where $\sigma$ is an arbitrary reference length that cancels from normalized probabilities. This removes the entropic contribution from the radial measure. This allows us to approximate $\tilde{F}^{3D}(r)$ as constant beyond a distance $R_{\text{far}}$ where interactions vanish.

Using this construction, the binding probability in a sphere of radius $L$ becomes

$$ P_{\text{b}}(L)=\frac{\int_{0}^{R_{\text{b}}}e^{-\tilde{F}^{3D}(r)}r^{2}P(b|r)\,dr}{\int_{0}^{R_{\text{far}}}e^{-\tilde{F}^{3D}(r)}r^{2}dr+\frac{L^{3}-R_{\text{far}}^{3}}{3}e^{-\tilde{F}^{3D}(R_{\text{far}})}}, $$

where $R_{\text{b}}$ is the largest distance at which $P(b|r)$ is nonzero, and $R_{\text{far}}$ is chosen in the noninteracting regime where $\tilde{F}^{3D}(r)$ is approximately constant. We define the dissociation constant $K_{\text{d}}$ as the concentration at which $P_{\text{b}}=1/2$ . Equivalently, if $L_{\text{d}}$ is the radius of the sphere whose volume gives half binding probability, then

$$ \frac{1}{K_{\text{d}}}=\frac{4}{3}\pi L_{\text{d}}^{3}. $$

### S3.2 Parametrization of the single-active-domain mBD2 model

The mBD2 variant is constructed to isolate the effect of reducing the number of active Ac-binding bromodomains while preserving the steric architecture of BRD4. Both BD beads are retained in the coarse-grained model, but BD2--Ac binding is disabled, so $n_{\text{d}}=1$ denotes one active Ac-binding domain rather than one physical BD bead.

To approximately match the effective BRD4–histone tail binding affinity of WT at intermediate acetylation ( $p_{\text{Ac}}=0.5$ ), the BD1–Ac well depth in mBD2 is increased by a factor of 1.131 relative to WT. All non-chromatin interactions are otherwise unchanged. A quantitative description of this matching procedure is provided in the caption of Fig. S9. Differences between WT and mBD2 are therefore interpreted as arising primarily from the reduction in active binding valency, with the effective affinity matched at intermediate acetylation.

### S3.3 Combinatorial binding model for multivalency

To understand how multivalency sharpens the dependence of co-condensation on acetylation density, we construct a combinatorial model of BRD4 binding to a nucleosome with multiple acetylatable histone tails. We seek an expression for the configurational partition function $Z$ describing multivalent BRD4 binding to an acetylated chromatin segment. The segment contains $N_{\text{Ac}}$ nucleosomes, each of which has $n_{\text{s}}$ acetylatable histone tails. Acetylation occurs independently at the level of individual tails with probability $p_{\text{Ac}}$ , so $N_{\text{Ac}}$ sets the size of the acetylated region, while $p_{\text{Ac}}$ controls the distribution of available binding sites on each nucleosome. Each BRD4 molecule contains $n_{\text{d}}$ active Ac-binding bromodomains, which determines the maximum number of simultaneous BD–Ac binding interactions in which a BRD4 molecule can participate. The full partition function $Z$ is constructed from contributions of individual nucleosomes, accounting for the combinatorial number of ways in which multivalent BRD4 molecules can occupy available acetylated sites.

#### Disorder-averaged configurational partition function.

We first consider whether a single BRD4 molecule can bridge two nucleosomes. The maximum separation at which such a configuration is geometrically possible is

$$ d_{\text{HH,interact}}\approx\sigma_{\text{HH}}+2D_{\text{g,H3}}+\frac{R_{\text{g,BRD4}}}{\sqrt{2}}, $$

where $\sigma_{\text{HH}}$ is the effective nucleosome size and $D_{\text{g,H3}}$ and $R_{\text{g,BRD4}}$ are the gyration sizes of the H3 tail and BRD4, respectively. Using $D_{\text{g,H3}}\approx l_{\text{AA}}\sqrt{37}\approx$2.3\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ and $R_{\text{g,BRD4}}\approx$6\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ gives $d_{\text{HH,interact}}\approx$19.4\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ , comparable to the nucleosome spacing $a_{\text{HH}}\approx$17\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ . However, forming two binding interactions at this distance requires highly specific geometries (alignment of two H3 tails and precise positioning of BRD4), leading to a substantial entropic penalty. We therefore assume that the net free-energy cost of inter-nucleosome bridging is unfavorable and neglect these configurations in the analysis that follows in this section. Under this approximation, nucleosomes can be treated as independent binding units. The total partition function then factorizes into a product of identical single-nucleosome contributions,

$$ Z=Z_{\text{H}}^{N_{\text{Ac}}}, $$

where $Z_{\text{H}}$ denotes the partition function for BRD4 binding to a single nucleosome.

We now consider a single nucleosome. Each nucleosome has $n_{\text{s}}=4$ acetylatable histone tails, each acetylated with probability $p_{\text{Ac}}$ . For the analytic model, we approximate acetylation on each nucleosome as independent across tails with probability $p_{\text{Ac}}$ , which yields the binomial distribution

$$ P_{k}=\binom{n_{\text{s}}}{k}p_{\text{Ac}}^{k}(1-p_{\text{Ac}})^{n_{\text{s}}-k}. $$

Because acetylation is quenched over a given chromatin realization, we use a disorder-averaged free energy

$$ -k_{\text{B}}T\ln Z_{\text{H}}=-k_{\text{B}}T\sum_{k=0}^{n_{\text{s}}}P_{k}\ln z_{k}, $$

where $z_{k}$ denotes the partition function of a nucleosome with $k$ available binding sites. This corresponds to the disorder-averaged single-nucleosome partition function

$$ Z_{\text{H}}=\prod_{k=0}^{n_{\text{s}}}z_{k}^{P_{k}}, $$

where $z_{0}=1$ by definition.

Given $k$ active sites, BRD4 molecules bind combinatorially. Each molecule has $n_{\text{d}}$ active Ac-binding domains ( $n_{\text{d}}=2$ for WT, $n_{\text{d}}=1$ for mBD2). We describe a class of binding configurations by a vector

$$ \vec{f}=\{f_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{m}\}, $$

where $m=|\vec{f}|$ is the number of bound molecules and $f_{i}$ is the number of domains used by molecule $i$ . The total number of occupied binding sites is

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}\leq k. $$

Binding via $n$ domains is characterized by an effective association volume $K_{n}$ . We approximate

$$ K_{n}\approx K_{1}\left(\frac{K_{1}}{v_{0}}\right)^{n-1}, $$

where $v_{0}$ is the effective interaction volume of a bound molecule. This approximation neglects geometric differences between binding configurations. It is justified by the fact that the size of BRD4 satisfies $R_{\text{g,BRD4}}\gtrsim d_{\mathrm{site}}$ , where $d_{\mathrm{site}}$ is the typical separation between acetylation sites on a nucleosome, so variations in stretching and entropic penalties between configurations are small.

We now enumerate configurations within a fixed filling vector $\vec{f}$ . A molecule binding through $f_{i}$ domains can choose which of its $n_{\text{d}}$ domains participate in $\binom{n_{\text{d}}}{f_{i}}$ ways. Binding sites are assigned sequentially: when assigning molecule $i$ , the previous molecules have already occupied $\sum_{q=1}^{i-1}f_{q}$ sites, so there are $k-\sum_{q=1}^{i-1}f_{q}$ available sites remaining, from which $f_{i}$ sites can be chosen. This gives a factor $\binom{k-\sum_{q=1}^{i-1}f_{q}}{f_{i}}$ . For each molecule, the $f_{i}$ selected domains can be paired with the $f_{i}$ selected sites in $f_{i}!$ distinct ways. If multiple molecules bind through the same number of domains, permuting those molecules does not generate a distinct filling. We therefore divide by the multiplicity factor

$$ R(\vec{f})!=\prod_{a}r_{a}!, $$

where $r_{a}$ is the number of molecules in $\vec{f}$ with $f_{i}=a$ . We group fillings by the total number of occupied sites. For a fixed total occupancy $j\leq k$ , we define $F_{n_{\text{d}},j}$ as the set of distinct filling vectors $\vec{f}$ whose entries are positive integers no larger than $n_{\text{d}}$ and whose entries sum to $j$ , with vectors related by permutation counted only once:

$$ F_{n_{\text{d}},j}=\left\{\vec{f}=\{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\}:1\leq f_{i}\leq n_{\text{d}},\;\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}=j\right\}/\,\text{permutations}. $$

The disorder-averaged single-nucleosome partition function is then

$$ \displaystyle Z_{\text{H}}(c) \displaystyle=\prod_{k=0}^{n_{\text{s}}}z_{k}(c)^{P_{k}}, \displaystyle z_{k}(c) \displaystyle=1+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{\vec{f}\in F_{n_{\text{d}},j}}\frac{1}{R(\vec{f})!}\prod_{i=1}^{m}(cK_{f_{i}})f_{i}!\binom{n_{\text{d}}}{f_{i}}\binom{k-\sum_{q=1}^{i-1}f_{q}}{f_{i}}. $$

Here, $z_{k}(c)$ sums over all distinct ways of occupying $k$ available binding sites with multivalent BRD4 molecules, including combinatorial choices of domains, binding sites, and their assignments, while $Z_{\text{H}}(c)$ averages this contribution over the distribution of acetylation states.

#### Adsorption isotherms.

We now compute the expected occupancy of BRD4 on a nucleosome from the partition function. The mean number of bound molecules is obtained as

$$ N_{\text{B}}(c,\dots)=c\frac{\partial\ln Z_{\text{H}}(c,\dots)}{\partial c}. $$

For the single-valent case ( $n_{\text{d}}=1$ ), this reduces to

$$ N_{\text{B}}(c,p_{\text{Ac}},K_{1})=4p_{\text{Ac}}\frac{K_{1}c}{1+K_{1}c}, $$

which has the form of a standard Langmuir adsorption isotherm. Here the factor $4p_{\text{Ac}}$ reflects the mean number of acetylated sites per nucleosome.

For the bivalent WT case ( $n_{\text{d}}=2$ ), a closed-form expression can be obtained for the simplified case $n_{\text{s}}=4$ with identical effective single-domain association volume $K_{1}$ and a single effective two-domain association volume $K_{2}$ , neglecting distinctions between H3/H4 tails and BD1/BD2 identities. Under these assumptions, the expression includes terms up to $(p_{\text{Ac}})^{4}$ :

$$ \displaystyle N_{\text{B}}(c,p_{\text{Ac}},K_{1},K_{2})=4p_{\text{Ac}}\frac{2K_{1}c}{1+2K_{1}c}+ \displaystyle+ \displaystyle(4p_{\text{Ac}})^{2}\frac{-3(K_{2}c)(2K_{1}c-1)}{4(1+2K_{1}c)((1+2K_{1}c)^{2}+2K_{2}c)}+ \displaystyle+ \displaystyle(4p_{\text{Ac}})^{3}\frac{3(K_{2}c)^{2}(2K_{1}c-1)}{2(1+2K_{1}c)((1+2K_{1}c)^{4}+8K_{2}c(1+2K_{1}c)^{2}+12(K_{2}c)^{2})}+ \displaystyle+ \displaystyle(4p_{\text{Ac}})^{4}\frac{-3(K_{2}c)^{3}(2K_{1}c-1)(5+20K_{1}c+6K_{2}c+20(K_{1}c)^{2})}{8(1+2K_{1}c)((1+2K_{1}c)^{8}+20(K_{2}c)(1+2K_{1}c)^{6}+120(K_{2}c)^{2}(1+2K_{1}c)^{4}+240(K_{2}c)^{3}(1+2K_{1}c)^{2}+144(K_{2}c)^{4})}. $$

#### Consequences for co-condensation sensitivity to acetylation density.

The effect of multivalency arises from the combinatorial growth in the number of binding configurations. For $n_{\text{d}}=1$ , the number of configurations scales linearly with the number of available sites $k$ . For $n_{\text{d}}=2$ , configurations scale combinatorially; for example,

$$ \binom{4}{2}=6>\binom{4}{1}=4. $$

As a result, highly acetylated nucleosomes contribute disproportionately to the partition function when multivalent binding is allowed. The enhancement becomes significant at the smallest $k$ for which multivalent configurations outnumber single-site configurations,

$$ k^{*}(n_{\text{d}})=\min\left\{k:\binom{k}{n_{\text{d}}}>\binom{k}{1}\right\}, $$

which gives $k^{*}=4$ for $n_{\text{d}}=2$ . Since $n_{\text{s}}=4$ , this threshold coincides with the maximal acetylation state of a nucleosome.

This has direct consequences for co-condensation. At low acetylation density $p_{\text{Ac}}$ , nucleosomes with $k\geq k^{*}$ are rare, and binding is dominated by effectively single-valent interactions. As $p_{\text{Ac}}$ increases, the probability of highly acetylated nucleosomes rises sharply, and these sites contribute more significantly to the binding free energy due to the combinatorial multiplicity of multivalent configurations. This produces a nonlinear increase in the effective binding affinity with $p_{\text{Ac}}$ , which in turn sharpens the dependence of BRD4 recruitment and co-condensation on acetylation density for WT relative to mBD2. This mechanism is consistent with the observation of a threshold-like increase in BRD4 assembly and co-condensation with increasing acetylation density.

### S3.4 Validation of combinatorial binding model using high-tension simulations

To isolate the combinatorial binding contribution from co-condensation effects, we perform simulations at high chromatin tension, where polymer deformation and co-condensation are suppressed. In this regime, BRD4 binding to chromatin is governed primarily by local binding interactions. We therefore compare simulation results to the combinatorial binding model by measuring the equilibrium occupancy of BRD4 as a function of acetylation density $p_{\text{Ac}}$ and saturation $S$ (Fig. S10). To remove trivial scaling with the number of available binding sites, we consider the normalized occupancy $N_{\text{B}}(S,p_{\text{Ac}})/(4p_{\text{Ac}})$ .

At low saturation ( $S\ll 1$ ), where BRD4–BRD4 interactions are negligible, the simulation results directly reflect the combinatorial binding mechanism. In this regime, WT BRD4 exhibits a strong increase of normalized occupancy with $p_{\text{Ac}}$ , while mBD2 shows little or no dependence on $p_{\text{Ac}}$ , consistent with the prediction that multivalency enhances the statistical weight of highly acetylated configurations. At higher saturation ( $S\sim 1$ ), both WT and mBD2 exhibit an apparent increase in occupancy with $p_{\text{Ac}}$ . However, this behavior is not captured by the combinatorial binding model alone and instead arises from cooperative BRD4–BRD4 interactions. This is confirmed by simulations of the mBD2-dC variant, which lacks the C-terminal domain responsible for these interactions and shows no such dependence on $p_{\text{Ac}}$ at high $S$ .

Together, these results demonstrate that the combinatorial binding model accurately describes BRD4–chromatin interactions in the regime where binding is dominated by local multivalency, while deviations at higher saturation arise from additional cooperative interactions not included in the combinatorial binding model.

## S4 Kinetics and rate calculations

### S4.1 Diffusion-limited timescale normalization

In the main text, rate densities are reported in diffusion-normalized units. Here we define the saturation-dependent simulation diffusion time used for that normalization; the mapping of this timescale to physical units is described in Section S2.1. To compare assembly formation rates across different saturation conditions, we normalize time by a characteristic diffusion timescale for BRD4 in the dilute phase. We define

$$ t_{\mathrm{Diff}}(S)=\frac{(2R_{\rm g})^{2}}{6D(S)}, $$

where $R_{\rm g}$ is the gyration radius of BRD4 measured in the dilute phase (and is approximately independent of $S$ ), and $D(S)$ is the center-of-mass diffusion coefficient of BRD4 at saturation $S$ . The length scale $2R_{\rm g}$ corresponds to diffusion over a molecular diameter.

In our simulations, diffusion arises from two contributions: stochastic forcing from the Langevin thermostat and collisional interactions between particles. Consistent with the model construction, these contributions are comparable in magnitude over the model parameter range of interest. The effective diffusion coefficient $D(S)$ is obtained from the long-time slope of the mean-squared displacement of BRD4 molecules in the dilute phase, averaged over particles and trajectories (Fig. S12). We find that $D(S)$ decreases with increasing saturation due to the enhanced rate of collisional interactions.

Using the computed $D(S)$ , we calculate $t_{\mathrm{Diff}}(S)$ and express all kinetic quantities in units of this timescale (Fig. S12). Unless otherwise stated, $t_{\text{Diff}}$ denotes $t_{\mathrm{Diff}}(S)$ evaluated at the saturation of the corresponding simulation. This normalization accounts for the saturation dependence of molecular diffusion and facilitates comparison between diffusion-limited and barrier-limited assembly regimes.

### S4.2 Measurement of assembly formation rates

#### Calculation of formation rate densities.

Assembly formation rates are extracted from ensembles of independent simulations initialized without pre-formed assemblies. For each trajectory, we define the first-passage time $t_{\text{1st-passage}}$ as the earliest time at which the assembly size exceeds the threshold used to identify formation of a stable assembly. The total formation rate for the simulated system is defined as

$$ J=\frac{1}{\langle t_{\text{1st-passage}}\rangle}, $$

where the average is taken over independent trajectories. Throughout this section, $J$ denotes a total rate for the simulated system, whereas $j$ denotes a rate density obtained by normalizing $J$ by the appropriate nucleation volume.

To compare rates across different saturation conditions, we normalize by the characteristic interparticle spacing in the dilute phase. Since $c_{\rm far}=Sc_{\mathrm{coex}}$ , the mean intermolecular distance scales as $c_{\rm far}^{-1/3}\sim S^{-1/3}$ , and the characteristic diffusion time across this distance scales as $S^{-2/3}$ . We therefore define the dimensionless diffusion-normalized rate density

$$ \tilde{j}(S,p_{\text{Ac}})\equiv\frac{j(S,p_{\text{Ac}})\,t_{\rm Diff}(S)}{c_{\mathrm{coex}}S^{2/3}}, $$

which factors out both the saturation-dependent molecular diffusion time and the expected concentration dependence associated with diffusion over the mean intermolecular spacing.

#### Calculation of off-chromatin rate densities.

For off-chromatin nucleation, rates are measured in homogeneous simulations at $S>1$ and converted to volumetric rate densities,

$$ j_{\mathrm{off}}=\frac{J_{\mathrm{off}}}{V}. $$

These rates are fit using the classical nucleation theory (CNT) form

$$ \ln\tilde{j}_{\mathrm{off}}(S)=A_{\mathrm{CNT}}-\frac{B_{\mathrm{CNT}}}{\ln^{2}S}, $$

where $A_{\mathrm{CNT}}$ and $B_{\mathrm{CNT}}>0$ are fit parameters. This expression reflects the expected CNT barrier scaling, $\Delta F^{*}/k_{\mathrm{B}}T\propto 1/\ln^{2}S$ , near coexistence. This fit is used to interpolate, and where necessary cautiously extrapolate, $j_{\mathrm{off}}(S)$ .

#### Calculation of on-chromatin rate densities.

For on-chromatin assembly, the appropriate normalization volume is not simply the full simulation volume because binding sites are spatially localized on chromatin. Approximating the relevant regions as cylindrical volumes around the chromatin fiber, the effective volume associated with the acetylated segment is

$$ V_{\text{Ac}}=N_{\text{Ac}}\,a_{\text{HH}}\,\pi\left(\frac{D_{\text{H}}}{2}+R_{\text{g,BRD4,gas}}\right)^{2}, $$

where $a_{\text{HH}}$ is the equilibrium nucleosome–nucleosome spacing, $D_{\text{H}}$ is the effective nucleosome diameter, and $R_{\text{g,BRD4,gas}}$ is the dilute-phase BRD4 gyration radius. The effective target volume $V_{\rm Ac}$ defined here is denoted by $v$ in the main text. The corresponding volume excluded by non-acetylated chromatin is

$$ V_{\text{non-Ac}}=(N_{\text{H}}-N_{\text{Ac}})\,a_{\text{HH}}\,\pi\left(\frac{D_{\text{H}}}{2}+R_{\text{g,tail}}\right)^{2}, $$

where $R_{\text{g,tail}}$ is the characteristic tail size used to estimate the excluded region around non-acetylated chromatin. Here $N_{\text{H}}$ is the total number of nucleosomes in the simulated chromatin fiber, and $V$ is the simulation volume.

The total measured rate in chromatin-containing simulations, $J$ , includes both chromatin-enhanced nucleation near acetylated segments and background homogeneous nucleation in the remaining accessible volume. We subtract the expected homogeneous contribution, $(V-V_{\text{non-Ac}})j_{\text{off}}$ , and normalize by $V_{\text{Ac}}$ to estimate the excess chromatin-associated rate density above the homogeneous background:

$$ j_{\text{on}}=\frac{J-(V-V_{\text{non-Ac}})\,j_{\text{off}}}{V_{\text{Ac}}}. $$

This construction provides an approximate chromatin-associated rate density while accounting for geometric exclusion and baseline homogeneous nucleation.

In regimes where assembly formation is not observed within the simulation time window, we report upper bounds on the total formation rate $J$ based on the total simulation time and number of independent trajectories, and convert these to the corresponding rate-density bounds using the same normalization conventions.

### S4.3 Analysis of nucleation and assembly formation rates

#### Analysis of nucleation rates above saturation ( $S>1$ ).

In this regime, formation proceeds via barrier-limited nucleation of a critical cluster of size $N^{*}(S)$ . Consistent with CNT, the normalized rate depends strongly on supersaturation, with $\ln\tilde{j}=A-B/(\ln S)^{2}$ near coexistence [24], as observed in both homogeneous simulations and in the presence of high-tension acetylated chromatin where co-condensation is suppressed. Increasing the acetylation density of high-tension chromatin enhances local BRD4–chromatin interactions and lowers the effective nucleation barrier, leading to increased heterogeneous nucleation rates. However, the dominant dependence on $S$ remains unchanged, indicating that the mechanism is still governed by barrier-limited nucleation.

#### Analysis of assembly formation rates below coexistence ( $S<1$ ).

Below coexistence, classical nucleation theory predicts that nucleation of the bulk condensed phase is thermodynamically unfavorable. However, in the presence of deformable chromatin, stable finite assemblies form via co-condensation. Assembly formation rates are observed to vary weakly with saturation once acetylation exceeds the threshold required for stable co-condensation. The diffusion-normalized rates $\tilde{j}$ collapse across saturation conditions, indicating that assembly kinetics are controlled primarily by diffusive transport rather than by a large nucleation barrier.

This behavior reflects a qualitatively different mechanism from nucleation-limited assembly. In the co-condensation regime, the dominant rate-limiting step is the diffusion of BRD4 molecules from the dilute phase to the chromatin region. Once bound, chromatin deformation and local stabilization proceed relatively rapidly, enabling growth without the need to overcome a large critical nucleus. We note that this does not imply the complete absence of barriers. At sufficiently low saturation, the system exhibits hysteresis, indicating the presence of a finite free-energy barrier. Rather, there exists a broad intermediate regime in which this barrier is sufficiently small that assembly formation appears approximately diffusion-limited, leading to the observed plateau in normalized assembly formation rates.

#### Comparison between multivalent and single-active-domain models.

The effect of multivalency on assembly kinetics is assessed by comparing WT BRD4 with the single-active-domain mBD2 variant. Above coexistence ( $S>1$ ), both models exhibit nucleation-limited kinetics with similar dependence on saturation, indicating that the dominant mechanism is barrier-limited nucleation. Differences between the models primarily reflect differences in effective binding strength. Below coexistence ( $S<1$ ), multivalency plays a qualitatively different role. WT BRD4 exhibits rapid assembly across a broad range of subsaturated conditions once acetylation exceeds the threshold for co-condensation, whereas mBD2 shows both reduced formation rates and a narrower range of conditions supporting assembly. These kinetic differences mirror the equilibrium behavior: multivalency enhances the sensitivity to acetylation density and expands the regime in which co-condensation is stable, thereby increasing both the accessibility and robustness of assembly under subsaturated conditions.

#### Dependence of formation rates on acetylation density.

Assembly formation rates as a function of acetylation density $p_{\text{Ac}}$ further illustrate the link between kinetics and equilibrium stability. At high chromatin tension, where assembly proceeds via nucleation, formation rates increase continuously with $p_{\text{Ac}}$ , consistent with a progressive reduction of the nucleation barrier. At low chromatin tension, where co-condensation is permitted, formation rates exhibit a threshold-like increase at a critical $p_{\text{Ac}}$ and then plateau over a broad range of subsaturation BRD4 concentrations. This plateau indicates a crossover to approximately diffusion-limited assembly and reflects the onset of stable co-condensation. For the single-active-domain mBD2 model, this threshold is shifted and the plateau is less pronounced, with formation rates more strongly suppressed at low saturation. This is consistent with the reduced ability of mBD2 to stabilize co-condensed assemblies. Overall, these results show that the dependence of assembly formation rates on $p_{\text{Ac}}$ directly tracks the onset and strength of co-condensation, linking kinetic accessibility to the same multivalency-driven mechanisms that govern equilibrium stability.

### S4.4 Absolute assembly timescales

We finally use the diffusion calibration established in Section S2.1 to estimate physical assembly-formation times. Using the dimensionless diffusion-normalized rate density defined in Eq. (S39), the corresponding physical rate density is

$$ j(S,p_{\text{Ac}})=\tilde{j}(S,p_{\text{Ac}})\,S^{2/3}\frac{c_{\mathrm{coex}}}{t_{\rm Diff}^{\rm exp}}. $$

From the bulk coexistence simulations, we obtain $c_{\mathrm{coex}}\approx$1744(\pm 87)\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{m}^{-3}$$ (Fig. S3), while Eq. (S9) gives $t_{\rm Diff}^{\rm exp}\approx$4.4(\pm 0.3)\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{s}$$ . Thus,

$$ j\approx$400(\pm 30)\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{m}^{-3}\mu\mathrm{s}^{-1}$\!\times\,\tilde{j}\,S^{2/3}. $$

In the co-condensation regime, the normalized formation rates approach a plateau of approximately $\tilde{j}_{\rm plateau}\sim 10^{-3}$ , corresponding to

$$ j_{\rm plateau}\sim$0.4\text{\,}\mu\mathrm{m}^{-3}\mu\mathrm{s}^{-1}$\!\times S^{2/3}. $$

To convert this rate density into an assembly-formation time for a specific acetylated chromatin region, we use the same effective target volume $V_{\text{Ac}}$ defined in Eq. (S42). For $N_{\text{Ac}}=20$ , with $a_{\text{HH}}=$17(\pm 3)\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ , $D_{\text{H}}\approx$10.6\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ , and $R_{\text{g,BRD4,gas}}\approx$6\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ , the effective radial extent is $D_{\text{H}}/2+R_{\text{g,BRD4,gas}}\approx$11\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$$ . The mean assembly-formation time is therefore

$$ \tau_{\rm assembly}=\frac{1}{V_{\rm Ac}j_{\rm plateau}}\sim$20\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$\times S^{-2/3}. $$

At $S=0.1$ , near the regime that provides optimal targeting in the main text, this gives

$$ \tau_{\rm assembly}\sim$90\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$. $$

These estimates should be interpreted as predicted first-passage times for the formation of a stable chromatin-associated assembly. A direct quantitative comparison with published live-cell measurements is not possible because existing experiments additionally depend on the number of available target sites and on detection thresholds. Nevertheless, the predicted subsecond assembly-formation time is compatible with the rapid, seconds-scale formation of BRD4 condensates observed in U2OS cells [16].
